meta.title: Who originally recorded "When the Levee Breaks"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Led Zeppelin. Kansas Joe McCoy and Memphis Minnie recorded it first, in New York on 18 June 1929, released by Columbia Records that autumn.
meta.ogTitle: Who originally recorded 'When the Levee Breaks'?
meta.ogDescription: Kansas Joe McCoy and Memphis Minnie cut it for Columbia in June 1929. Led Zeppelin's 1971 rearrangement is a cover — and it leaves McCoy off the credit.

answer.label: Not a Led Zeppelin original — a 1929 Kansas Joe McCoy and Memphis Minnie single on Columbia
answer.originalArtist: Kansas Joe McCoy and Memphis Minnie
answer.originalArtistDates: Kansas Joe McCoy 1905–1950 · Memphis Minnie 1897–1973 · American country blues duo, married 1929
answer.sourceLine: The riff, the hallway drums and the seven-minute sprawl are Led Zeppelin’s, but the song is not. “When the Levee Breaks” was written and first recorded by Kansas Joe McCoy and Memphis Minnie, cut in New York City on 18 June 1929 and issued by Columbia Records that August or September, with “That Will Be Alright” on the other side. McCoy sang and played rhythm guitar; Minnie, the stronger guitarist, supplied the finger-picked embellishments. Led Zeppelin’s 1971 rearrangement credits Memphis Minnie alongside the four band members — but not McCoy, whom Charles Shaar Murray identifies as the song’s actual writer.

original.charted: Did not chart. It was sold into the segregated ‘race records’ market and, as American Songwriter puts it, “didn’t have much of an impact at the time” relative to the duo’s other sides.

original.cover: Led Zeppelin’s rearrangement closes their untitled fourth album, released by Atlantic Records on 8 November 1971. It was never issued as a single; the album reached No. 1 in the UK and No. 2 on the US Billboard 200.

trail: Wikipedia’s article on the song ↗ gives the 18 June 1929 New York session, the Columbia release in August–September 1929, the “That Will Be Alright” B-side, and notes Charles Shaar Murray’s identification of McCoy as the writer.

MusicBrainz ↗ keeps the 1929 country blues work, credited to Memphis Minnie and Kansas Joe McCoy, separate from the Led Zeppelin work credited to the band plus Minnie — the two are distinct entities in the database.
Louder ↗ describes the original’s two-guitar arrangement and states plainly that the Led Zeppelin credit names Memphis Minnie although McCoy wrote it.
American Songwriter ↗ records that the 1929 single made little impression at the time, and that the credit on the 1971 label carried Memphis Minnie’s name alongside the band’s.

authors.name: Kansas Joe McCoy and Memphis Minnie
authors.heading: Kansas Joe McCoy & Memphis Minnie
authors.metaLine: Kansas Joe McCoy, b. 11 May 1905, Raymond, Mississippi; d. 28 January 1950, Chicago. Memphis Minnie, b. Lizzie Douglas, 3 June 1897, Tunica County, Mississippi; d. 6 August 1973, Memphis.
authors.bio: A Columbia talent scout reportedly found the pair busking outside a Memphis barber shop, and a company A&R man handed them the stage names they kept for life. They married in 1929, the same year they travelled to New York for their first session, and recorded as a duo for Columbia and Vocalion until the partnership — and the marriage — came apart in the mid-1930s. Minnie went on to a recording career spanning three decades and roughly 200 songs; McCoy’s most durable composition turned out to be “Why Don’t You Do Right?”, a jazz standard by way of Lil Green, Benny Goodman and Peggy Lee.

authors.name: Led Zeppelin
authors.heading: Led Zeppelin
authors.metaLine: English rock band, formed London 1968. Jimmy Page, Robert Plant, John Paul Jones, John Bonham.
authors.bio: Their rearrangement closes the untitled fourth album, released by Atlantic Records on 8 November 1971. The band had failed to make the song work at Island’s Basing Street studio; it came together at Headley Grange, where engineer Andy Johns set John Bonham’s kit in the stone-walled hallway and hung a single stereo microphone from the second-floor landing. Page layered guitars, backwards harmonica and backwards echo over it, and the basic track was slowed down for weight. The result is one of the most sampled drum recordings ever made — and the reason most listeners assume the song began in 1971.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: The confusion here is not that a band recorded someone else’s song — it is that the rearrangement is so total that the source vanished, and the printed credit only names half of it.

items.why: The version on the untitled fourth album is so radically rebuilt — slower, longer, and famous for its drum sound — that it is routinely taken for an original composition.

context.heading: Why the 1971 version swallowed the 1929 one
lead: The original is a mid-tempo country blues built on two guitars: McCoy’s loose, almost ragtime rhythm underneath, Minnie’s dancing lead on top in an open tuning. It runs a little over three minutes, because that is what a 78 rpm side held. It sold into the ‘race records’ market of 1929, made no lasting commercial impression, and was one of a whole shelf of blues records the Great Mississippi Flood of 1927 produced — Lonnie Johnson and Barbecue Bob had already been to the studio with flood songs of their own.

Led Zeppelin did not so much cover it as rebuild it. The tempo dropped, the melody changed, the arrangement stretched past seven minutes, and the drum sound — a room, a stairwell and one microphone — became a piece of production folklore in its own right. When a record is that thoroughly reconceived, the source tends to disappear behind it. The credit on the sleeve did the rest: Memphis Minnie’s name appears there, McCoy’s does not, and the version most people can hum is the one with a 1971 date on it.
detailsBody: April 1927 — the Great Mississippi Flood; levee failures displace hundreds of thousands across the Delta. Blues records about the flooding begin appearing within days.
18 June 1929 — Kansas Joe McCoy and Memphis Minnie record “When the Levee Breaks” in New York City for Columbia Records. McCoy sings and plays rhythm guitar; Minnie plays the finger-picked lead.
August–September 1929 — Columbia issues the 78, backed with “That Will Be Alright”. It is the duo’s first release for the label.
1971 — Led Zeppelin cut a heavily rearranged version at Headley Grange, Hampshire, with Bonham’s drums recorded in the hallway. It is the only track on the album mixed at Sunset Sound in Hollywood.

8 November 1971 — released by Atlantic Records as the closing track of Led Zeppelin’s untitled fourth album. Never issued as a single; the album reached No. 1 in the UK and No. 2 on the US Billboard 200.
Composer credit on the Zeppelin recording reads Bonham, Jones, Memphis Minnie, Page and Plant — McCoy’s name is absent.
context.pull: The drums are 1971. The song is 1929.
